Welcome toSliding Pulses

One pulse slides across another: what value does their convolution take at each shift?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: the convolution of the rectangular pulse with itself as the area of an overlap, traced one shift at a time

About this simulation

On screen
Top, against x′ from −5 to 5: the fixed pulse Π(x′) in black, the reflected and shifted sliding function g(x − x′) in blue (its top edge drawn slightly raised), their overlap shaded grey at the height of the product, and −w, w, x − w, x + w under the edges. Bottom, against the shift x from −3.5 to 3.5: a black dot at (Π ∗ g)(x) with a dotted drop line, and the blue trace of every shift visited.
Controls
Drag the blue function (or use the Shift slider) to set x from −3.5 to 3.5. ▶ Play sweeps x to 3.5 at 0.5 per second, from −3.5 if it is already at the end. The half-width w and the sliding function (pulse Π or averaging window Π/2w) clear the trace; x is kept.
Measured
The dot height is read by linear interpolation from Ops.convolveFFT of the pulses sampled every 0.001; the overlap runs from max(−w, x − w) to min(w, x + w), and its length is shown beside the value. The Shift box beside the slider takes a typed value, rounded to the slider’s 0.05 steps.

Overlap and the value it givesΠ(x′), g(x − x′) against x′ · (Π ∗ g)(x) against x

Guided Inquiry

1 · Widening both pulses

Set the half-width to w = 0.5, the sliding function to the pulse Π and the shift to x = 0, so that the blue pulse lies on the black one and the dot reads 1. Before raising the half-width to w = 1, keeping the shift at x = 0, predict (Π ∗ Π)(0). Then raise it and read the value at the dot.

2 · Sliding off

Keep w = 1 and the pulse. Before dragging the blue pulse from x = 0 to x = 1, predict how the dot moves. Then drag it and watch the dot and the grey area.

3 · Where the overlap ends

Keep w = 1 and the pulse. Before dragging further to the right, predict the smallest shift at which the dot reaches 0. Then drag and check.

4 · Shifting the other way

Keep w = 1 and the pulse, with the shift at x = 2. Before dragging the blue pulse to the left, to x = −1, predict (Π ∗ Π)(−1). Then drag it there and read the value at the dot.

5 · The whole sweep

Set the half-width to w = 1.5, keep the pulse, and press ▶ Play in the top bar to sweep the shift from −3.5 to 3.5. Before pressing it, predict the traced curve.

6 · An averaging window

Set w = 1, switch the sliding function to the averaging window Π/2w and set the shift to x = 0, where the dot reads 1. Before dragging the window to x = 1, so that its centre sits on the right edge of the black pulse, predict the reading of this averaging instrument. Then drag it there and read the value at the dot.

7 · Convolution as a sliding overlap

(Π ∗ g)(x) = ∫ Π(x′) g(x − x′) dx′: reflect g, slide it by x, multiply the two functions and take the area of the product.

Two pulses of half-width w give the triangle 2w − |x|, of height 2w and zero beyond |x| = 2w: convolution widens and smooths.

With a window of unit area, Π/2w, the convolution is a running mean, like a measuring instrument that blurs sharp edges.

Explore freely: drag the blue function, change w and the sliding function, and watch the trace build up.

Sliding One Pulse across Another

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A black pulse of half-width w stays put while a second pulse, drawn in blue, is reflected, slid along by a shift x and laid over it. The sim shades their product and plots one dot against x: the convolution at that shift.

What you'll learn

  • How a convolution is built by reflecting, sliding and multiplying.
  • What the dot in the lower graph measures at each shift.
  • How the half-width w and the choice of sliding function change the result.
The sim's layout. Upper panel, plotted against x′: the fixed pulse, the sliding pulse and the grey product. Lower panel, against x: the dot, with the trace of the shifts visited behind it.

What's on screen

  • The upper panel shows Π(x′) in black, the sliding function g(x − x′) in blue (its top edge drawn slightly raised, to tell coinciding edges apart) and the grey product. Under the axis are −w, w, x − w and x + w.
  • The lower panel plots the convolution against x. The dot sits at the current shift, and the blue trace covers the shifts already visited.
  • Readouts: the shift x, the overlap in x′, the overlap length and the value (Π ∗ g)(x).
See itLook at the sim as it opens. Watch for: the black and blue pulses in the upper panel and the dot in the lower one.

03

The convolution is an integral of a product, with one function reflected and slid by x

The convolution of two functions f and g is defined by (notes, eq. 6.33):

(f ∗ g)(x) = ∫−∞∞ f(x′) g(x − x′) dx′
The convolution integral.

To form the integrand, g is reflected, so that g(−x′) is drawn against x′, and then shifted a distance x to the right. That is the blue curve g(x − x′) in the upper panel. Multiplied by the fixed f(x′), it gives the product the sim shades grey, and the value at that shift is the area under the product.

Here f is the rectangular pulse Π, equal to 1 for |x′| < w and 0 elsewhere. The sliding function g is either the same pulse or the pulse divided by its width 2w. The lower graph plots the area against x as the shift moves.

Key idea. Every point of the lower graph is one area, found for one position of the blue curve.
See itDrag the blue pulse a little to the right, or set x = 0.6. Watch for: the grey shape and the dot both changing as the blue pulse moves.
04

At zero shift the overlap is the whole pulse, so the value is 2w

For the pulse Π both heights are 1, so the product Π(x′)Π(x − x′) is 1 where the two pulses overlap and 0 elsewhere. Its area is then the length of the overlap (notes, after eq. 6.33).

At x = 0 the blue pulse lies exactly on the black one, the overlap runs from −w to w, and (Π ∗ Π)(0) = 2w. At the opening w = 1 the dot reads 2. At w = 0.5 it reads 1, and at w = 1.5 it reads 3. The reading is a length, not the height of either pulse, which is 1 throughout.

Zero shift at two half-widths. The grey overlap is the whole pulse, and its length is the value of the dot.
Key idea. The value is the overlap length, 2w at zero shift, and not the height 1 of the pulses.
See itSet w = 1 and x = 0. Watch for: the overlap running from −1 to 1 and the dot reading 2.
See itNow set w = 0.5, keeping x = 0. Watch for: the overlap length and the dot both falling to 1.
05

The overlap falls in a straight line from 2w at x = 0 and ends at |x| = 2w

For 0 < x < 2w both conditions, |x′| < w and |x − x′| < w, hold on x − w < x′ < w, an interval of length 2w − x. At w = 1 that is a straight line from 2 at x = 0 to 1 at x = 1, with no flat stretch. The overlap ends when the left edge of the blue pulse, x − w, reaches the right edge of the black one, w. That is x = 2w, or x = 2 at w = 1, and the value stays 0 beyond it.

w = 1 and x = 1. The blue pulse covers 0 to 2, so the overlap with the black pulse is 0 to 1.

The same argument holds for −2w < x < 0, so (Π ∗ Π)(x) = 2w − |x| for |x| < 2w and 0 beyond. Both pulses are even: at x = −1 the value is 1, as at x = 1.

The value for w = 1. The points are the ones quoted in the text.
Key idea. The value falls by exactly as much as the shift grows, in either direction, and is zero once |x| reaches 2w.
See itSet x = 1, keeping w = 1. Watch for: the overlap running from 0 to 1 and the dot reading 1.
See itMove on to x = 2. Watch for: no grey region left and the dot reading 0.
See itGo the other way, to x = −1. Watch for: the overlap running from −1 to 0 and the dot reading 1, as at x = 1.
06

The result is a triangle of height 2w and base 4w, taller and wider as w grows

Π ∗ Π is the triangle of the notes' Figure 54: zero until −2w, rising to 2w at the centre, and back to zero at 2w. The peak is the overlap of a pulse with itself, and the base is twice as wide as either pulse.

Three half-widths. The peaks are 1, 2 and 3, and the half-bases 1, 2 and 3.

Raising w from 0.5 to 1.5 takes the peak from 1 to 3 and the half-base from 1 to 3. At w = 1.5 the sweep from x = −3.5 stays at 0 until x = −3, peaks at 3, and is back to 0 at x = 3. Two pulses of half-width w give a shape of half-width 2w: convolution widens.

x w g

These controls move the sim's too, and a change of w or g clears its trace.

Key idea. The triangle has height 2w and half-base 2w, so a wider pulse gives a taller and wider result.
See itSet w = 1.5 and press ▶ Play to sweep the whole range, or look at the finished sweep here. Watch for: a triangle from −3 to 3, with the dot at x = 0 reading 3.
07

An averaging window of height 1/2w makes the value a mean over its width

If g is the pulse Π divided by its width 2w, then (f ∗ g)(x) is the mean value of f over an interval of width 2w centred on x (notes, §6.2). It could describe an instrument that averages what it measures over a finite range.

The window slid to x = 1, so that its centre sits on the right edge of the pulse.

The window has height 1/(2w) and unit area, so the value is the overlap length times 1/(2w). At x = 0 the whole window lies on the pulse and the mean is 1. At x = 1 and w = 1 the window covers 0 to 2, only half of it lies on the pulse, and the dot reads 1/2. The trace is (2w − |x|)/(2w), a triangle of height 1 for every w.

Key idea. A unit-area window makes the convolution a running mean, so at the pulse's edge it reads one half.
See itChoose the window with w = 1 and set x = 1. Watch for: half of the window over the pulse and the dot reading 0.5.
See itWiden the window to w = 1.5 and look at the finished sweep. Watch for: the same triangle shape, still of height 1, now from −3 to 3.
08

Summary

In one line. The sim reflects one function, slides it across another and plots the area of their product against the shift.
  • Pulse with itself: (Π ∗ Π)(x) = 2w − |x| for |x| < 2w, and 0 beyond.
  • It is a triangle of height 2w and base 4w, so its peak is the overlap length and not the height 1.
  • Window Π/2w: the same triangle divided by 2w, a mean over the window, with height 1.

Common mix-ups

  • "Both pulses have height 1, so the convolution is 1." At x = 0 and w = 1 the dot reads 2, the overlap length.
  • "The value stays at the peak until the pulses separate." It starts falling at once: 1 at x = 1, and 0 only at x = 2.
  • "A negative shift gives a negative value." At x = −1 the dot reads 1, the same as at x = 1.
  • "The window reads the value at its centre." At x = 1 its centre is on the pulse's edge and it reads 1/2, the mean over its width.

Things to try on your own

  • Set w = 0.75: the peak is 1.5 and the value reaches 0 at |x| = 1.5.
  • Choose the window at w = 0.5 and x = 0.5: half of it lies on the pulse, so it reads 0.5.
